          Mass Overhaul or Squad Continuity: What is the Recipe for Premier League Success?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 8, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author, Ithiel Piñero / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
In an age when fans wants limitless spending on shiny new signings, we ask whether less change can sometimes be more beneficial.
If a cautionary tale was needed for a football club assuming the grass is always greener on the other side, Tottenham Hotspur’s experience so far in 2026-27 may well do the job.

After a dismal 2025-26, in which Spurs escaped relegation by the skin of their teeth, the club dived head first into their hopes for a shiny new era on the back of Roberto De Zerbi’s insistence the squad needed immediate, severe and costly surgery. After De Zerbi saved the club from the drop, he was handed the keys to a weighty war chest, and he spent big.

Upwards of £300 million was dished out and more or less an entire new team was brought in. Spurs signed 10 new players who have all gone into the first team; just five league games into the new season and all nine of the outfield signings have made at least one appearance in the Premier League, while many of them are already key players.
You don’t need a deep data dive to see it hasn’t worked yet. Spurs are bottom of the table without a win five games into 2026-27. It’s their worst start to a Premier League season.

It might all work out in the end. Spurs might become world beaters with this squad. Or even if it doesn’t go quite that well, they could feasibly become a half-decent team very soon indeed. This season obviously isn’t a complete write-off already.

But even if they do turn things around, by making such a poor start, they have given everyone else a head start. Spurs are playing catch-up with every other team, and now face a 33-game run in which they have to make up a deficit if they are to retain their Premier League status. They need to improve drastically to make the season anything like a success.

In fairness to De Zerbi, the evidence of the last two seasons was pretty strong. Spurs had finished 17th twice consecutively, last season playing some utterly miserable football while suffering a string of serious and debilitating injuries, and the squad clearly needed new additions. But has too much been changed too suddenly?

Spurs have become only the 12th team in Premier League history (excluding promoted teams) to hand more than 25 starts in the space of the first five games of a season to players who didn’t play for the club the previous year.

The concern for Spurs is, historically, doing that doesn’t go well. Six of the previous 11 have ended up finishing 17th or lower in the first season after the summer overhaul. Only one has finished higher than ninth.
Many of those teams were arguably always destined to be in a relegation battle and had attempted to avoid as much by making a lot of summer signings, such as QPR in 2012-13 or Portsmouth in 2005-06.

Spurs finished fifth as recently as 2023-24 and would have been hoping to get back into the elite quickly, but they are, whether they like it or not, a relegation-battling side. And the early evidence of this season along with the history of other clubs who have made this much change doesn’t bode well for them.
So, are these numbers and Spurs’ troubles the sign of a wider problem with significant player turnover? Were they wrong to approach the summer with this aggressive approach to the transfer market?

First up, it’s worth noting that there are examples of teams signing lots of players and things working out, if not always immediately, then in the long term. Nottingham Forest broke the record for the most players signed by a Premier League club after winning promotion in the summer of 2022 and have since established themselves as top-flight regulars (although they were later deducted four points for breaching the Premier League’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules). Chelsea transformed their squad and fortunes after Roman Abramovich arrived at the club. Sunderland qualified for Europe last season after a summer of overhaul following their promotion.

But there are many more examples of teams struggling after making a lot of signings, as is the case with many of the sides in the above table who gave lots of starts to new signings early on in the new season.
And this term, too, the teams who have started well are generally those who have not overhauled their squad.

Of the eight teams to give 10 or fewer starts to players who didn’t play for them last season, five are better off than the position in which the Opta supercomputer predicted they would finish before the start of the campaign. In other words, when comparing season-to-season changes in the starting XI with performance relative to (the supercomputer’s) expectations, teams who didn’t make many alterations are doing well.

And it’s the opposite at the other end of the spectrum. Of the eight teams who have given at least 13 starts this season to new players, all but one are currently in a lower position than they were in the Opta supercomputer’s pre-season predictions.

Whether by complete coincidence or not, there appears to be a correlation between the two. A greater number of new players this season has led to underperformance compared to what the supercomputer foresaw for that team.

There are a few obvious outliers. Bournemouth have given fewer starts to new players (five) than any other team in the Premier League this season (though they do have a new manager), but they are currently seven places lower than their predicted position from pre-season.
